Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown

instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC notes — `task-feaa278f`

## Rule: replicate the marked tile into blank matching panels

A full-color divider cross partitions the grid into equal rectangular panels (the dividers themselves remain). One panel/tile contains a sparse pattern on an otherwise uniform background; copy that tile's pattern into corresponding positions in the other panels. The mapping is by equal local row/column offsets (translation with orientation preserved), not a geometric reflection. Keep divider lines unchanged and preserve the grid dimensions.

### Demo evidence

Demo grid was 15x11, with background 8, a full horizontal divider of 1 at row 7, and a full vertical divider of 1 at column 5. The upper-right 7x5 panel held the pattern. Output copied each cell of that panel, at identical local coordinates, into the upper-left, lower-left, and lower-right panels; divider row/column stayed 1. For example, upper-right row-local 3 was `[8,8,8,3,6]`, and output put that same sequence at columns 0–4 as well as 6–10 in both corresponding 7-row bands. No mirror/reversal was applied.

### Solved recurrence/test evidence

Test grid was 23x5, with vertical divider color 2 at column 2 and horizontal divider rows 7 and 15. The middle band (rows 8–14) contained the pattern in the two-cell-wide tile to the right of the vertical divider:

`[1,3], [6,6], [1,1], [9,1], [1,1], [1,8], [1,1]`

(background 1; divider color 2). The output replicated this 7x2 tile at columns 0–1, retaining its local left-to-right order, and repeated the band into rows 0–6 and 16–22. Dividers stayed unchanged. This was accepted correct with 0 wrong submissions.

### Practical solve

1. Identify full horizontal/vertical divider lines and partition the grid into equal-sized panels.
2. Find the panel containing non-background marks (or the marked band if the partitions tile a larger region).
3. Copy its local pattern to the other corresponding panels, aligning top-left/local coordinates; do not reverse columns or rows.
4. Preserve divider color and exact dimensions. When multiple panels contain marks, combine the populated tile information to form the shared tile before filling blank corresponding panels.

### Distinction to watch

The demo's source upper-right pattern was copied directly into left/bottom panels; this is alignment-preserving tiling, not mirror symmetry about the dividers. In the test, a right-side mark at column 4 mapped to column 1 in the left two-column panel because both correspond to local column 1 within their respective tiles.

## Additional solved evidence: replicate one tile in both dimensions (task recurrence, 2026-09-29)

A fresh instance with a 17x11 grid had divider columns 3 and 7 (color 4) and divider rows 5 and 11 (color 4), making a 3x3 arrangement of 5x3 panels. The 5x3 tile at rows 6–10, columns 0–2 contained background 1 plus marks: local `(row 0,col 2)=7`, `(row 1,col 0)=9`, `(row 2,col 1)=7`. The accepted output copied this entire tile, same orientation and local offsets, to every panel at row starts 0, 6, 12 and column starts 0, 4, 8, leaving divider rows/columns intact. This instance was solved after one incorrect submission.

Important correction: replication is two-dimensional across all matching panels, not only horizontally within the initially marked band. Do not infer a tile's full content from the grid's blank-looking panels; use the marked tile as the pattern and repeat it across panel rows and columns. The demo was 11x5 with divider row 3 and column 2 (color 2), 3x2 panels of size 3x2. Its source tile's non-background content was `[[6,6],[8,1],[1,1]]`; the output tiled that pattern in all six panels. This confirms whole-tile repetition over both axes.
